messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
Adeola has worked hard to build a life of precision and order. At twenty, she is a newly qualified pharmacist, a role she takes pride in, finding comfort in the clear logic of prescriptions and the quiet hum of the dispensary. But for the last eight months, this carefully constructed world has felt impossibly fragile. The terror that broke into her life during a humanitarian aid trip has followed her home, leaving shards of memory that pierce the quiet moments of her days. The event itself resists language; when Adeola tries to speak of it, the words catch in her throat. It exists for her not as a story, but as a series of disjointed sensory snapshots: the rough texture of a concrete floor, the echoing shouts of angry men, and the suffocating, overwhelming rush of water. She feels it more than she remembers it.

This bodily memory ambushes her without warning. Last week, a heated argument broke out between a couple waiting for a prescription. As their voices escalated, Adeola froze behind the counter, her hands hovering over a blister pack. The shouting seemed to fill the room, and suddenly she was no longer in the pharmacy. A wave of cold washed over her, and she felt an phantom pressure on her chest, her back arching involuntarily against the stool as if fighting a physical weight. Her breath caught, a dry, rasping gasp, and for a moment she was convinced she was drowning. When her colleague touched her shoulder, she flinched violently. She couldn't explain what had happened, only that the rest of her shift was spent in a state of high alert, her eyes constantly scanning the faces of customers for any sign of threat.

This feeling of being perpetually on guard has become her baseline. Adeola has come to believe that safety is an illusion and that catastrophe is always one moment of inattention away. Before starting any task at work, even just restocking shelves, she identifies the nearest two exits. When she and her boyfriend go out for dinner, she insists on a table where she can see the door, her gaze sweeping the room every few minutes. At home, sleep offers no respite. She lies awake for hours, straining to hear any unfamiliar sound, certain that she must remain vigilant. The exhaustion is profound, but the alternative—the nightmares that wait for her in sleep—feels worse. In them, the water returns, and she is powerless, forced into positions she cannot escape. To keep them at bay, she stays up late, scrolling endlessly on her phone until she collapses from sheer fatigue.

The trauma has also carved out a space of profound guilt and self-recrimination. She knows others were there with her, and the fact that she survived while they did not feels like a debt she can never repay. This thought often hardens into a conviction: she tells herself she deserves to suffer. It is a punishment she silently enacts, a way to balance some cosmic scale that feels horribly askew. This belief system makes connection feel impossible. When her boyfriend, trying to be helpful, insists she let him handle a difficult phone call, the feeling of her autonomy being taken away is so terrifying it triggers a silent panic. She has started avoiding people who remind her in any way of her captors—a man with a similar build on the bus, a stranger with the same accent—crossing the street or ducking into a store to evade them.

She has sought therapy because the walls are closing in. Her manager has spoken to her about her distraction, and her boyfriend grows more distant, frustrated by a pain he cannot see or understand. Adeola is terrified of speaking about what happened, convinced that if she allows the full, coherent memory to surface, it will utterly dismantle her. But the life she is living now, a fragmented existence governed by fear and avoidance, is becoming its own kind of prison. Her greatest hope is simple and seemingly unattainable: to one day feel safe in her own body, in a quiet room, with the door closed.
